newsitem.title: CHINA: China envoy in HK meets Tung, assures no meddling.
newsitem.headline: China envoy in HK meets Tung, assures no meddling.

text.p: The new chief of China's Hong Kong watchdog met post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa on Thursday and assured him the agency would not meddle in his government.
Jiang Enzhu, director of the Xinhua News Agency branch, told Tung during their first official meeting that his office would not interfere in the running of local affairs.

However, Jiang said the Xinhua office, the Chinese Communist Party's Hong Kong base, would continue to maintain contacts with Hong Kong people from all walks of life in order to improve ties, according to a government statement.

At the same time, the head of Hong Kong's administration, Chief Secretary Anson Chan, praised the head of China's new Foreign Ministry office in Hong Kong for honouring a pledge not to meddle in the territory's affairs.
Chan also said Hong Kong would hold "fair and open elections" next year, so that the territory's 6.4 million people would have a legislature that truly represented them.
Ma Yuzhen, the head of China's Foreign Ministry in Hong Kong, "has made it quite clear... that he would not interfere in the activities in Hong Kong," she told reporters.
"I can say, in practice, that he has done exactly that. He has not interefered...so I am delighted we are off to a good start with Mr Ma," she said.
Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule on July 1 after 156 years of British control and is now a special autonomous region with a high degree of autonomy, except in diplomacy and defence.
Ma's office handles Hong Kong's external affairs and serves as a channel to Beijing, while Xinhua will remain the Chinese Communist Party's base in Hong Kong.
Xinhua acted as a watchdog and shadow government in the colonial era. Its deputy directors were like shadow ministers tracking specific policy areas.
This role is likely to be greatly reduced now that Hong Kong is ruled by a China-backed government.
Chan denied that the government's plan to scrap the British electoral set-up would slash the chance of pro-democracy candidates in next May's Legislative Council election.

"I like to stress that we have no wish to boycott or make it more difficult or indeed to make it easier for any individual of any political party to participate in the election. We are aiming for fair and open election," she said.
Pro-democracy campaigners have blasted the China-backed government for changing the voting system to proportional representation from first-past-the-post.
